hook_text: Some of the energy in your plug is 250 million years old, and once it's burnt, it's gone forever.
clip_script: Flip a switch in South Africa, and most of the power comes from coal. That coal was once a swamp forest, 250 million years ago. Burn it, and it's gone. That's a non-renewable resource, like a box of matches. Gold, platinum, oil: same story. South Africa's gold mines now dig more than three kilometres down. Now look up. The sun will rise again tomorrow, and the wind will blow. Use them all you like. That's renewable. But here's the twist. Fish, forests, soil and water are renewable too, like a fruit tree that gives fruit every year. Cut the tree down, and the fruit stops. Take too much, and even a renewable resource can disappear. The question isn't just what we use. It's how.
visual_style: A light switch; a coal power station with steam; a fossil leaf in coal; a deep gold mine shaft; a solar farm in the Northern Cape; wind turbines on a coastal hill; a fruit tree full of fruit, then a stump; a shoal of fish.
pacing: Quick contrasts, slowing for the twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources.
